newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Samper blames job loss on drug war.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Samper blames job loss on drug war.

text.p: For the second time in less than a week, President Ernesto Samper said on Monday that Colombia's soaring unemployment rate was one of the side effects of the country's fight against the drug trade.
"We have unemployment because we're making ethical adjustments to the economy," Samper said in a national radio and television address.

"It true that many jobs have been lost to this fight," he added, saying drug money was no longer being used to build luxury apartment buildings and hotels or to provide equipment for farms owned by billionaire traffickers.

The National Statistics Department reported last week that Colombia's urban unemployment rate had hit a nine-year high of 12.7 percent in the first quarter, up 2.5 percent from the same period last year.
Cali and Medellin, the cities that gave their names to two of Colombia's most notorious drug cartels, had the highest rates of unemployment at 17.4 and 16.4 percent respectively.
Joblessness is said to be nearly double the urban rate in Colombia's countryside, and Samper said rural areas had suffered from efforts to "clean up the economy" as well.
Until recently, he said about 25 percent of Colombia's arable land was controlled by criminal drug gangs.
"Five of the 20 million hectares (49.4 million acres) of arable land were in the hands of organized crime," he said.

He did not say how much of that land had been confiscated by the authorities, but he suggested that much of it was now lying fallow thanks to stepped-up efforts to crush the country's criminal drug syndicates.
"For many years, a number of activities -- construction, tourism and some agroindustries among them -- were infiltrated by drug money," Samper said.

The embattled president, clearly sensitive to charges that he has done too little to create new sources of employment, did not refer to allegations that his own 1994 election campaign was heavily infiltrated by cocaine cash.
